snippet.title: Mount Rushmore - The Unfinished Masterpiece
snippet.description:
Mount Rushmore may be one of the world’s most iconic landmarks, but it isn’t actually finished. Gutzon Borglum’s original design envisioned each president carved down to the waist—not just the heads we see today.

He also began work on a hidden Hall of Records - a tomb-like chamber behind the mountain intended to house important documents - but it was never completed.

With the outbreak of World War II, funding and labour were redirected, bringing work to a halt. Borglum died in 1941, leaving behind an ambitious vision that remains only partially realised.

snippet.title: How US Marine Special Operations Actually Work | Authorized Account | Insider
snippet.description:
Nick Jones is a former US Marine Raider who served in MARSOC, the Marine Corps’ elite special operations unit.

After starting his career as an infantry mortarman and scout sniper, Jones went on to complete the rigorous Marine Raider training and deployed multiple times to Iraq and Jordan. In 2020, Jones was awarded the Navy Cross for his actions during a chaotic firefight with ISIS fighters in northern Iraq in which he repeatedly charged into enemy fire to rescue wounded teammates despite being shot in the leg himself.

Jones speaks with Business Insider about Marine Raider selection, advanced infantry tactics, and operating alongside allied forces. He goes into detail about the intense realities of close-quarters combat and the firefight that led to his Navy Cross. Jones also reveals the mental and physical toll of combat, detailing his personal struggles with trauma, injury recovery, and alcoholism.

Following his retirement from active service, Jones has dedicated his career to supporting the veteran community. He is the founder of the Talons Reach Foundation, a nonprofit based in Jackson Hole, Wyoming.

snippet.title: Europe's First Chapter: The Geological Birth Of A Continent
snippet.description:
Europe was not born in a single moment. In Expedition Europe: Birth Of A Continent, geologist Colin Devey follows the deep-time story written into Europe's rocks, seas and mountains. On the Isle of Lewis, 2.9 billion year old gneiss reveals the ancient nucleus of the continent, while Scotland's seas connect today's wildlife to the explosion of life 540 million years ago. At Loch Ness, the Great Glen Fault marks the collision of Laurentia and Baltica around 450 million years ago.

The journey continues through the Central Uplands, where the Variscides helped unite Europe around 350 million years ago and later gave rise to the coal that powered industrialization. In Portugal, 152 million year old dinosaur fossils reveal a time when Europe and North America still shared close links before the Atlantic opened around 220 million years ago. From the volcanic Azores to the Urals and the Manpupuner pillars, this documentary uncovers how Europe became a continent.

snippet.title: D-Day's Untold Heroes: The Men Behind History's Greatest Images - Full History Documentary
snippet.description:
On June 6, 1944, thousands of soldiers stormed the beaches of Normandy. But alongside them were another kind of warrior—men carrying cameras instead of rifles, risking their lives to capture the images that would define World War II forever. 📽️ 

On June 6, 1944, the largest amphibious invasion in history began.

More than three million Allied troops, thousands of ships and aircraft, and an immense logistical operation launched the assault that would become known as D-Day.

The battle has been told countless times.

But few know the extraordinary story of the men who landed with cameras instead of weapons.

Combat photographers, filmmakers and journalists followed the first assault waves onto the beaches of Normandy, exposing themselves to the same machine-gun fire, explosions and chaos as the soldiers they accompanied. Some never returned. Others captured images that would become among the most iconic photographs and films of the Second World War.

How did they survive the invasion? How did they film under enemy fire? And how did those precious reels of film make their way from the battlefield to the world?

Drawing on three decades of research, exceptional archives from the U.S. National Archives, personal diaries, family collections and remarkable wartime footage, this documentary uncovers the forgotten heroes who preserved the visual memory of D-Day.

Through the stories of legendary filmmakers including John Ford, George Stevens, Jack Lieb and Walter Rosenblum, experience Operation Overlord from an entirely new perspective—through the lenses of the men who risked everything to ensure history would never be forgotten.

If you enjoy uncovering hidden chapters of history, don’t forget to like 👍, subscribe 🔔, and share to support more documentaries like this!

snippet.description:
After the Martin PBM Mariner went down during Operation Highjump, six crew members were stranded in Antarctica with temperatures around –20 °C. A rescue from USS Pine Island was initially impossible due to the brutal weather.

As days passed and rations dwindled, morale plummeted. On day seven, a search plane flew nearby but couldn’t spot them through poor visibility.

snippet.title: China’s Earliest Binary Coding Machine
snippet.description:
You may think that a silk dress and binary coding have very little to do with one another, but actually they’re more closely related than you think.

Long before computers existed, silk weavers were already working with systems that worked a lot like digital code. On early looms, a series of pedals, shafts, and beams controlled the threads: press a pedal and a shaft lifts; release it and the threads fall back into place.

Each movement determined which strands of silk rose and which stayed down, shaping the pattern thread by thread. By combining these motions in different sequences, weavers could create incredibly complex designs.

snippet.title: How Television Was Invented
snippet.description:
in 1926, John Logie Baird built one of the first working television systems. At its heart was a spinning disk with 30 holes arranged in a spiral pattern. As the disk rotated, each hole scanned a different line of an image, breaking it down into a sequence of light and dark signals.

These signals were transmitted and used to control a light source on a second synchronized disk at the receiver. As that disk spun in perfect time, it reconstructed the image line by line. 

The result was a crude, flickering picture, but it proved that moving images could be sent through the air, laying the groundwork for modern television.

snippet.title: Police shoot a man near elementary with a knife
snippet.description:
Sacramento, CA - The Sacramento Police Department on Sunday night released body camera footage of an officer shooting a suspect near an elementary school last month in the Northgate area.

Police said the incident began around 6:45 p.m. on March 10 when dispatch received a call that a man was on a school campus along the 3100 block of Northstead Drive, armed with a knife and would chase anyone who approached him.

The police department redacted the school's name from the video, but the scene and report of the call were near Hazel Strauch Elementary.

The Sacramento County Sheriff's Office's helicopter was able to locate the suspect walking in front of the school and holding a knife, the video shows. Police said the deputies were telling the suspect to drop the knife.

The video shows the suspect walking toward an officer as the officer was pointing a gun at the suspect.

The department said officers made multiple commands for the suspect to drop the knife and tried to de-escalate the situation, but they said the suspect refused and continued toward the officers.

This is when at least one officer fired their weapon. Police said a less-lethal conducted energy device was also deployed at the same time.

The suspect was then detained and officers provided medical aid. Officers said in the video that the suspect suffered one gunshot wound to the stomach.

The suspect, later identified as 29-year-old Jamal Dearmond of Sacramento, was taken to a hospital before he was booked into jail for multiple counts with a deadly weapon.

Police said it was determined that the suspect was the person who called dispatch regarding the disturbance. A knife was located at the scene
